history_title: The people and documents behind the colonial claim
history_content:
A Native homeland before a colonial title

Rockaway is the peninsula between Jamaica Bay and the Atlantic Ocean in southern Queens. Its Native place name predates the English ownership documents. William Wallace Tooker's historical compilation records seventeenth-century spellings and an account of a Rockaway village in 1643. These records make an inhabited coastal homeland visible before the later patent. They should not be read as a complete account of Native life or as evidence that the community ended when a colonial title was issued. The Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent

Who made the 1685 claim?

John Palmer acquired a deed bearing the marks of Pamon and Tackpousha, whose names appear in different spellings in later publications. The deed was dated October 6, 1685, acknowledged on October 9, and recorded at Palmer's request on October 27. A New York court's 2017 opinion quotes the earlier 1916 title examination distinguishing these dates. Recording a document and making an agreement were separate acts; October 27 should not simply replace the deed's date. Nassau Point Lagoon, Inc. v. Burrell

English colonial governor Thomas Dongan then issued Palmer a patent on November 3, 1685. Alfred Bellot's 1917 history recounts the patent and its annual payment of a bushel of wheat to the colonial government. This was an English governmental claim to authorize and recognize private title over an existing Native homeland. It was not merely an exchange between two private individuals. History of the Rockaways

An ownership claim that other settlers disputed

Hempstead's competing claim complicated Palmer's acquisition. Bellot reproduces Dongan's February 1687 defense against allegations of favoritism: the governor said Hempstead inhabitants could object and described a survey intended to distinguish the disputed territory. These are Dongan's arguments defending his administration, not independent proof that Native people freely accepted every consequence of the transaction. The conflict also shows colonial officials and settlers negotiating among themselves over authority to allocate Native land. History of the Rockaways

On August 23, 1687, Palmer transferred his Rockaway interest to Richard Cornell, also written Cornwell, an ironmaster from Flushing. Within two years, the claim had passed through a Native deed, the English governor's patent and another private transfer. Those successive instruments help explain how colonial control became an inheritable and transferable property claim. History of the Rockaways

What a deed can—and cannot—tell us

A title chain records the claims that later owners and courts relied on. By itself, it cannot establish what every Native signer understood, whether coercion shaped the agreement, or which relationships to land continued outside its written terms. The named parties and the actual provisions matter. This chapter does not assume that the Rockaway agreement reserved exactly the same fishing, planting or gathering rights documented in other Long Island deeds.

The broader land-loss explanation below distinguishes resource-use rights from private ownership and connects these documents to colonial governmental power. It also introduces LandBack as restoration of Indigenous authority and relationships, with examples attributed to the communities leading them.

Native presence is not confined to the title record

An English patent is not an endpoint for Indigenous history. In the wider New York region, Lenape Center's contemporary leadership includes Joe Baker and Curtis Zunigha, enrolled members of the Delaware Tribe of Indians, whose work includes arts, education and agriculture. Their present work offers a way to learn from living Native people rather than treating colonial property papers as the last word. This regional connection does not assign all Rockaway descendants to one organization. About Us
whereintheworld_content: The outline follows the modern Queens portion of the Rockaway Peninsula, using New York State shoreline boundaries. It locates this chapter beside Jamaica Bay and the Atlantic; it does not reproduce the 1685 deed or survey. The modern Queens–Nassau line is an orientation limit, not an asserted historic Native boundary. The peninsula's western shoreline changed substantially after the seventeenth century, so today's coast cannot establish the extent of the original claim.
